pulls.title: kernel: Use typed errors for fatal and flush error notifications
pulls.body:
Part of the libbitcoinkernel project (tracking issue #27587 ), specifically the "Remove translation.h usage from the kernel" item. `kernel::Notifications::fatalError()` and `flushError()` take a `bilingual_str`, which pulls `util/translation.h` and the application-level `G_TRANSLATION_FUN` into the kernel library, and translation is an application concern rather than a consensus one. The same interface already shows the way out: `warningSet()` takes a `kernel::Warning` enum, and the node turns it into a translated string in `node/kernel_notifications.cpp`.

Along with removing the dependency, another goal here is separating responsibilities, because the goals of error handling and error reporting are different: presenting an error to a user is an application concern, not something `libbitcoinkernel` itself should own. The error is structured on both sides: in C++ as the full `kernel::FatalError` variant, and in the C API as its numeric value. With the current changes the C side only carries half of that structure today though, the dynamic fields (a block hash, a path, an exception's `what()`) do not cross the C API yet, even though ideally they should.

This PR does the same for the two error notifications. A new `src/kernel/error.h` defines `kernel::FlushError` as a plain enum and `kernel::FatalError` as a `std::variant` with one struct per error, whose fields carry the context the message needs: a block hash, a path, the `what()` of a caught exception, block heights. It holds types and nothing else, so every message is now built on the node side. The exception is `FatalErrorString()` in `validation.cpp`, because a fatal error raised during validation also fails the block through `BlockValidationState::Error()`, which takes the reason as a plain string right there, and `fatalError()` returns void, so the node has no way to put its message into that state. A follow-up could store the typed error in the state instead and let the node create the string message.

This does not remove the kernel's dependency on `util/translation.h`, it is just a step. The other two notifications, `progress()` and `warningSet()`, still take a `bilingual_str`, and `bitcoinkernel.cpp`, `checks.cpp`, `node/chainstate.cpp`, `txmempool.cpp` and `validation.cpp` still include the header.

There is one behavior change to mention here. The two C API callbacks lose their `message` parameter, so they now carry only the error code, the same pattern that `btck_BlockValidationResult` already uses.

pulls.title: validation: don't accept txs to the mempool while loading a snapshot
pulls.body:
`ActivateSnapshot` checks that the mempool is empty before it starts, but `PopulateAndValidateSnapshot` then runs without `cs_main`, which takes minutes on mainnet. A transaction entering the mempool in that window (e.g. through `sendrawtransaction`) hits the assert in `AddChainstate`:

```
Assertion failed: (!prev_chainstate.m_mempool || prev_chainstate.m_mempool->size() == 0), function AddChainstate, file validation.cpp, line 6201.
```

By then the base blockhash file has been written, so the node needs `-reindex` to start again.

This sets a flag on `ChainstateManager` while `ActivateSnapshot` runs, and `AcceptToMemoryPool` and `ProcessNewPackage` reject with `snapshot-loading` while it's set. `testmempoolaccept` still works. A second `loadtxoutset` started while one is running is also rejected.

`test_mempool_blocked_during_load` in `feature_assumeutxo.py` pauses the load through a FIFO, checks that `sendrawtransaction` and `submitpackage` are rejected and the mempool stays empty, then lets the load finish. On master the transaction is accepted and the node aborts. The test is skipped where `os.mkfifo` isn't available.

pulls.title: Configuration argument handling improvements.
pulls.body:
Several numeric configuration options now reject values that are out of range instead of silently wrapping or inverting. Previously a negative value could disable the intended limit entirely.

  - `-dbbatchsize` and `-dbcrashratio` must be non-negative. A negative `-dbbatchsize` wrapped to a huge value and disabled batch flushing, so a reindex could hold an unbounded batch in memory.
  - `-limitclustersize`, `-limitancestorcount`, `-limitdescendantcount`, `-mempoolexpiry`, `-datacarriersize`, `-maxsendbuffer`, `-maxreceivebuffer`, `-bantime`, `-bytespersigop` and `-maxtipage` must be non-negative.
  - `-limitclustercount` must be between 1 and 64.
  - `-timeout` must be positive. It previously fell back to the default silently, unlike the analogous `-peertimeout`, which already errored.

  Zero remains valid wherever it already meant "disabled": `-dbbatchsize=0`,
  `-limitclustersize=0`, `-datacarriersize=0`, `-mempoolexpiry=0`,
  `-maxtipage=0`, `-bytespersigop=0`, `-maxsendbuffer=0`,
  `-maxreceivebuffer=0` and `-bantime=0`.

- The `-help` output for `-bytespersigop`, `-datacarriersize`, `-dbbatchsize`, `-stopatheight` and `-checkblockindex` now shows the `=<n>` placeholder for their value, matching how they are actually parsed.

pulls.title: p2p: replace full outbound peers that don't support tx relay (take 2)
pulls.body:
Picks up #28538

Outbound-full-relay slots should be used by peers that actually relay transactions, besides #28538 see #16418 and #28371 for the motivation. So try to replace peers that are not relaying txs with peers that do.

The approach differs from the original PR in a few details in response to some of the review comments there:

- A replacement is connected before the peer is evicted. The original PR disconnected a non-tx-relaying peer once all full outbound slots were filled. Reviewers preferred having a replacement available first (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). Now an extra outbound-full-relay connection is requested, like the extra network-specific peers, and the existing eviction of extra outbound peers prefers peers that don't relay txs.
- Peers not relaying txs don't get `m_protect`. Otherwise they could stay forever (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443336121), and ignoring the protection was rejected in the same thread (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443312604).
- An only peer on a network is not replaced. Otherwise the network-specific extra connections and this logic would keep replacing each other (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). This also covers the `-maxconnections=1` case (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1417178196).

Nothing is changed in `-blocksonly` mode or during IBD. The rename commit and the functional test are taken from the original PR with some changes to match the new behavior.

pulls.title: rpc: fail scanblocks when block filter range is unavailable
pulls.body:
### The issue

`scanblocks` reads block filters over a range via `LookupFilterRange`. When the
block filter index is behind the active chain (e.g. right after startup, while
it is still syncing in the background), the lookup for the not yet indexed range
fails. The old code ignored that failure, advanced `start_index` to the end of
the chunk, and kept going - so the scan skipped every unindexed block and still
returned `"completed": true`.

The result is a silent gap: a caller gets a `relevant_blocks` list that looks
fine but is missing any match in the unindexed range, with no way to
distinguish "no matches" from "range was never scanned".

Note that `"completed"` only means the scan was not aborted - it does not mean
every filter in the requested range was actually read.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start a node with `-blockfilterindex=1` and let it mine/receive some blocks.
2. Stop the node, delete `<datadir>/<chain>/indexes/blockfilter`, restart with
   `-blockfilterindex=1`.
3. Immediately (before the index finishes rebuilding) call
   `scanblocks start '["addr(<addr>)"]'`.

Before this change the call returns `"completed": true` with an empty/partial
`relevant_blocks`, silently skipping the range the index had not rebuilt yet.

### How it is fixed and why

Mirror `getblockfilter`'s error classification:

- Call `BlockUntilSyncedToCurrentChain()` only to obtain an `index_ready` flag.
  Do **not** fail unconditionally when the index is still behind the tip - the
  requested range may already be available.
- If `LookupFilterRange` fails and the index is not ready, throw the same
  "still in the process of being indexed" `RPC_MISC_ERROR` that
  `getblockfilter` uses.
- If `LookupFilterRange` fails after the index is ready, throw
  `RPC_INTERNAL_ERROR` (unexpected / corruption), instead of skipping the chunk.

This closes the silent gap without rejecting scans whose range is already
covered while the index catches up to the tip.

The diff also reindents the match loop: inverting `if (LookupFilterRange(...))`
into an early `throw` removes one nesting level from the existing body. That
reindentation is a consequence of the bug fix, not a standalone style change.

### Tests

- `test/functional/rpc_scanblocks.py` - new `test_scanblocks_unindexed_range`
  covers the modified code: it pads the chain, wipes the filter index, restarts,
  and while the index is behind the tip asserts that a scan to the tip returns
  the indexing error, that a scan over an already-written prefix (genesis)
  still succeeds, and that after sync the match is found.
- The existing `run_test` cases (which `wait_until(... synced ...)` before
  scanning) continue to exercise the normal synced path.

### AI / tooling note

I found this regression while reviewing the RPC with an AI-assisted tool.
I reproduced the unsynced-index behavior myself, chose to mirror
`getblockfilter`'s existing guard, and verified the fix with the
functional test above. This PR text and any review replies are my own.

pulls.title: compressor: oversized script decoding can leave a spendable script
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The oversized-script fallback appends `OP_RETURN` to the destination instead of replacing it. If the destination already contains an unfinished push, the appended byte becomes pushed data and the result can remain spendable.

**Fix:** Replace the destination with `OP_RETURN` rather than appending it.

Found while reviewing #36280. This predates that PR and appears latent because oversized outputs are excluded from the UTXO set, but it could affect malformed stored records decoded into a reused destination.

Encrypting existing wallets that are unencrypted is fraught with footguns and complexity both for users and for developers.

For example:

- No efforts are made to ensure that remnants of unencrypted key material are not left on the user's disk, as attempting to ensure this would be difficult and dangerous, and for some SSD's infeasible.

- Encrypting a wallet that has manually imported descriptors will cause the wallet to change the spending conditions out from under the user. (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/26607)

pulls.title: http: support unix sockets
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/5029

Accept unix socket paths as options for `-rpcbind=` (server) and `-rpcconnect=` (bitcoin-cli). Options follow the same pattern as `ipcbind`:

- `=unix` is a magic keyword that means `<datadir>/http.sock`
- `=unix:relative/path` means `<datadir>/relative/path`
- `=unix:/absolute/path` means `/absolute/path`

We delete any existing `http.sock` before calling `bind()` and do not clean up at shutdown.

Because access is handled by the filesystem, `-rpcallowip` is ignored for unix sockets and not required at all if we are *only* binding to unix sockets.

Authentication by username/password/cookie is still required.

A new option `--httpunix` is added to the test framework and added to test_runner for `rpc_bind.py` and `interface_http.py` for CI, but (like `--usecli`) most other tests should also pass with that option. When set, bitcoind is started with `-rpcbind=unix...`which overrides `tcp://localhost` entirely. `AuthProxy` has been extended to connect directly to the unix socket.

Try it out!
```
bitcoind -regtest -rpcbind=unix
bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcconnect=unix getbestblockhash
```

Refactored code:

Back in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27375 we added unix socket support but it was isolated to the `Proxy` class. That created a bit of tech debt which we pay off in this PR. Two new classes are implemented:
- `UnixSocketAddr` reflects the `CService` API for generic unix sockets, without bitcoin-p2p-specific attributes
- `SocketAddr` holds a variant of `UnixSocketAddr` and `Cservice` so classes like `Proxy` and `HTTPServer` can operate on an abstract level, with either socket type.
- `CNetAddr` and `CService` are left untouched -- they are somewhat dirty combinations of generic socket classes and bitcoin p2p code, adding unix sockets to those classes wouldn't make sense for bitcoin p2p operations and that's why this design was chosen.

Follow-up suggestions:
- Deduplicate some of the unix socket path resolution code between IPC and HTTP
- On macos the default unix socket buffer size is only ~8k. In the functional tests we have to bump the python client socket buffer up to ~256k or the "throttle" tests will stall on macos. We could apply this socket option on the server side as well, only on macos... requires some bike shedding.
- This option replaces TCP but it does not replace HTTP, there may be a more efficient transport protocol.


Production code and test framework changes designed and authored by my own cranial meatball. Unit tests added by Opus. C++ cleaned up by Fable, security tightened by Kimi-k3 🧠 🤖 🤖 🤖

pulls.title: validation: fix false corruption errors after pruning or AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `getblockfrompeer` restores a pruned block's body without recreating its undo record. If startup verification reaches that block at level >2, it attempts to disconnect it and reports database corruption, preventing the node from restarting.

**Fix:** Stop deep verification when a pruned node reaches missing undo data, using the existing result for unavailable history. The same allowance covers missing undo on AssumeUTXO snapshot chainstates, matching the existing treatment of unavailable snapshot history. Level 4 still reconnects the newer blocks that were disconnected. `verifychain` returns false to indicate incomplete verification. Lower verification levels and corruption checks for undo records marked as present retain their existing behavior.

This came up during [pruned `txindex` review](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002). The pending `pruneassumevalid` change also needs verification to handle missing undo correctly, so this fix is being split out to land first.

pulls.title: Test: Add legacy script edge case spender test
pulls.body:
Move the spender framework from feature_taproot.py to test_framework/spenders.py, and use it in a new feature_legacy_script.py test for script edge cases that other implementations have gotten wrong: CSV with -2, a 5-byte operand whose value fits in 1 byte, IFDUP on negative or non-minimal zero, ROLL with duplicate values, OP_16 in a P2SH scriptSig, and a P2SH scriptSig that leaves 1,000 items for the scriptPubKey to run on.

pulls.body:
This applies the txindex key scheme from #35531 to `txospenderindex`. The motivation is to save space and to allow replicating what #36002 does for `txindex`, by referencing blocks instead of local files.

The first commits refactor the index code so the #35531 scheme can be shared: `BaseIndex::DB` can opt in to the versioned sync locator, and the block sequence keys, sequence assignment and salted hasher move from txindex into `index/block_seq.h`, without changing txindex's on-disk format. The following commits switch txospenderindex to the new keys and add tests. As in txindex, entries of disconnected blocks are kept and lookups only count blocks in the active chain, so `CustomRemove` is gone. Entries written by v31 are still read as a fallback. The last commit makes `FindSpender` skip candidates it cannot read and return `std::optional`, mimicking `TxIndex::FindTx`, since with 5-byte prefixes an unreadable false positive could otherwise hide the real spender.

Each entry is about 33% smaller (key bytes):

- before: 's' (1) + SipHash-2-4 of the outpoint (8) + CDiskTxPos, as varints nFile (2) + nPos (4) + nTxOffset (3) = 18 bytes
- after: 'x' (1) + SipHash-1-3-UJ prefix (5) + block sequence varint (3) + tx offset (3) = 12 bytes

I did not have time to do a benchmark (my setup is really cheap, laptop where i work with an external SSD connected), will try to do on the next days. But same as #35531 i hope to reduce disk space and indexing time.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: reject duplicate coins and empty snapshot groups
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Snapshot loading doesn't validate the announced coin count against the unique UTXOs loaded.
Repeated outpoints collapse into one coin, so a snapshot can repeat every record, announce the doubled count, and still match the committed UTXO hash.
`loadtxoutset` then reports the inflated count as `coins_loaded`.

Snapshot loading also accepts transaction groups with no coins.
They leave the UTXO hash unchanged and don't advance the coin count, so parsing them bypasses the interrupt check and can delay shutdown.

**Fix:** Compare the announced count with the unique coin count already produced by the existing UTXO statistics scan, and reject zero-count transaction groups while parsing the snapshot.
When both the content hash and coin count are wrong, loading reports the hash error first.

pulls.body:
**Problem:** Loading a UTXO snapshot on a pruned node can leave the active tip without block or undo data. Attempting a rollback with `dumptxoutset` then triggers an assertion and terminates the node.

**Fix:** Reuse `GetPruneHeight` to reject rollback with the existing pruning error when the required data is unavailable.

pulls.title: interfaces: Avoid node crashes from invalid Chain IPC calls
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A program using the `Chain` IPC interface from #29409 can crash `bitcoin-node` with a single bad call: asking for a block hash above the tip, passing a negative height to `hasBlocks`, leaving the transaction argument of `broadcastTransaction` or `checkChainLimits` unset, or returning an error from a notification handler. Separately, `findAncestorByHash` reports success when the descendant block is unknown (#36472). The `Chain` methods were written for in-process C++ callers like the wallet, which follow documented preconditions, so they assert or dereference null instead of returning errors.

**Solution:** Make these `Chain` methods in `src/node/interfaces.cpp` return errors for invalid arguments, catch and log IPC errors from notification handlers, and fix the `findAncestorByHash` check. Three small commits, each with unit tests in `src/test/interfaces_tests.cpp`. Valid calls behave the same as before. Details are in the commit messages.

This PR does not depend on #29409, but the fixes matter if it is merged and `interfaces::Chain` is exposed over IPC. The problems were reported by zaidmstrr, willcl-ark and xyzconstant while reviewing #29409, by enirox001 in #36472, and by cyb3ralbert and xyzconstant here (`hasBlocks`). The `findAncestorByHash` fix is the same one previously proposed by Romansage6 and Yudis-bit in #36473, #36484 and #36490.

Fixes #36472.

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization, while becoming very slow to deserialize.

This PR stores the stack as its serialization in a single allocation (or none if the stack is empty), with a small header holding its size and the offset of the last element. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place, only allowing replacing them entirely. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead. `CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes.

Later commits also introduce stricter checking during deserialization, rejecting the following before fully deserializing:
* Transactions with more inputs/outputs than are possible in a valid transaction.
* Transactions with 0 inputs or 0 outputs (applied in P2P, but not RPC etc. for backward compatibility).
* Transactions/blocks that exceed the 4M weight limit (also only applied in P2P).

The result is a significant reduction in the worst-case time and memory allocations needed for deserialization, both in valid and invalid transactions. With it, the worst-case memory of a valid deserialized block drops from 106.8 MiB to 6.0 MiB. Memory usage during deserialization can temporarily be higher: up to 7.8 MiB for valid blocks, and up to 13.4 MiB for invalid blocks, which can combine a few temporary vector allocations of up to 5 MB each.

Deserialization time and memory of the deserialized block, master → PR. Runtimes are medians in milliseconds. Memory usage is in MiB, and ✕ means rejected at deserialization time. Peak memory refers to the memory during deserialization itself, not persisted in the deserialized `CBlock` object. Numbers over 50 ms, 20 MiB usage, or 100 MiB peak are in **bold**.

| block | gcc | clang | mem | peak mem |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Valid blocks** |
| 1 tx, max 1-byte wit elems | **99.1** → 16.0 | **111.4** → 21.9 | **106.8** → 3.8 | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, max empty wit elems | **279.2** → 18.7 | **293.7** → 25.1 | **91.5** → 3.8 | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout, 1-item wit | 12.33 → 13.39 | 15.00 → 15.43 | 6.7 → 6.0 | 6.7 → 6.0 |
| max txs, 1 txin and 1 txout | 6.43 → 7.04 | 7.87 → 8.30 | 5.8 → 5.6 | 5.8 → 5.6 |
| 1 tx, max txins, 1-elem wit | 4.53 → 4.68 | 5.04 → 5.37 | 4.0 → 2.9 | 4.0 → 2.9 |
| mainnet block 969729 | 5.30 → 5.47 | 5.97 → 6.20 | 3.5 → 2.9 | 3.5 → 2.9 |
| **Invalid blocks** |
| 400k txs, many wit elems, truncated | **84.8** → 16.1 | **95.6** → 21.8 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 12.6 |
| 400k txs, big wit+scriptsig, truncated | **84.0** → 16.1 | **96.0** → 21.7 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 13.4 |
| 1 tx, 2M 1-byte wit elems | **98.0** → 10.6 | **109.9** → 16.2 | **106.8** → ✕ | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, 4M empty wit elems | **271.0** → 13.4 | **288.9** → 19.6 | **91.6** → ✕ | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max empty txs | **101.0** → 0.006 | **139.0** → 0.008 | **67.1** → ✕ | 67.1 → 4.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout | 27.6 → 7.3 | 34.5 → 8.5 | **23.4** → ✕ | 23.4 → 6.4 |

So in addition to improving worst cases very significantly, it also provides modest memory usage improvements to the common case. This translates to mildly increasing the effective capacity of memory-bounded data structures that store transactions, like the mempool.

Some notable changes:
* By implementing some checks (for inherently consensus-invalid things) in the deserialization logic, behavior may change. In particular, deserialization errors in P2P cause messages to be dropped/ignored, rather than triggering validation or net processing logic (which may include disconnections and/or inserting into reject filters).
* The rejection of transactions with too many inputs or outputs applies everywhere, including in RPC. That's hopefully a desirable change, but a change in behavior still.
* Random access to the witness stack elements becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$. This is not a problem for any validation logic, but may be relevant for the libbitcoinkernel API which exposes an individual element accessor.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

There are a few possible follow-ups:
* Enforce the 400k WU policy limit during transaction deserialization when active (instead of the 4M WU consensus limit).
* Extend this approach to entire `CTransaction`, allowing all transaction data to be stored packed together in a few allocations (rather than one per input, one per output, one per witness) plus some index structure to access it efficiently. That's a much bigger change, needing abstractions like #35569, but would reduce the maximum memory usage per WU for valid blocks from around 1.5 bytes/WU to 1.1 bytes/WU (compared to ~28 bytes/WU in master).

pulls.title: mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pulls.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: allow retrying loadtxoutset after an interrupted load
pulls.body:
**Problem:** An interrupted `loadtxoutset` can leave an incomplete `chainstate_snapshot` database without its required `base_blockhash` marker. A later call can fail to open that database, requiring the operator to remove it manually before retrying.

**Fix:** Wipe the snapshot database before opening it so a later call can replace incomplete data. LevelDB acquires the database lock before deleting files, so a database held open by another load cannot be wiped. Also correct the startup warning to identify the missing marker and explain that retrying replaces the directory.

pulls.title: validation: check the most recent AssumeUTXO commitment during IBD
pulls.body:
**Problem:** AssumeUTXO verifies imported UTXOs against a hash we bake into the binary.
Every node reconstructs the same UTXO set during ordinary IBD, but [does not check its hash against the existing AssumeUTXO commitment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32377).

**Fix:** During ordinary block validation, verify the AssumeUTXO hash when block connection reaches the corresponding block.
Log mismatches and raise a GUI/RPC warning while allowing IBD to continue.
Flush pending changes to disk before hashing the UTXO set and comparing the result with the commitment.

Keep only the latest AssumeUTXO commitment per network to limit the extra hashing work during IBD, and update the release process to replace it.
Users who need older snapshots for research or other purposes can use a compatible older release or restore the corresponding commitment as `m_assumeutxo_data` and recompile.

pulls.title: net: serve `MSG_BLOCK` by stripping witnesses in place
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Serving blocks to legacy nodes currently decodes and reserializes them just to remove witnesses. `MSG_WITNESS_BLOCK` already avoids this work by serving the stored bytes directly. Faster witnessless IBD, as proposed in [#36476](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36476), also needs peers to serve these blocks efficiently.

**Fix:** Read disk-backed, non-Signet `MSG_BLOCK` replies into an owned byte buffer, check the header's proof of work and expected hash, and strip witness ranges from that buffer in place.

Extract a shared helper so decoding transactions and skipping their bytes follow the same encoding rules. Signet keeps `ReadBlock` for its solution check. Header checks now precede transaction parsing, so records corrupted in both places can log a different error.

**Performance:**

Time to read a block from disk and build its non-witness message:

| Block | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `block413567` | 1.31 ms | 0.147 ms | **8.9x** |
| Same block with synthetic witnesses | 3.47 ms | 0.374 ms | **9.3x** |

The synthetic fixture adds a 512-byte witness item and an empty item to every input.

**Related work:** This extends the raw witness-block serving added in [#13151](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13151). The [#13011 discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13011#issuecomment-383145046) and the closed [#13098](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13098) identify unnecessary transaction hashing when serving historical blocks. The implementation also builds on the bulk block reads introduced in [#31551](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31551).

**Problem:** Full chainstate compaction can temporarily require nearly another copy of the database before old files are deleted.

**Fix:** Log automatic full compaction start and finish at info level. Skipping avoids the temporary extra disk use but leaves obsolete data taking up space.

Fixes #36585

pulls.title: [Demo] validation: remove AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Draft demo:** this is meant to showcase what complete AssumeUTXO removal could look like and the simplifications that AssumeUTXO currently prevents.
The decision about complete removal is of course still open. This draft is meant to serve as a concrete reference for the smaller proposals below - it's not meant to be merged.

**Smaller PRs:** I will carve out individual changes to gauge interest in each part, and link them here as they are opened.
Some of the findings are useful even if snapshot loading or background validation stays.
Feedback on which parts seem worth pursuing, and in which order, is welcome.

**Motivation:** this follows our in-person discussion at the October 2026 Core Dev meeting.
My impression was that there was rough agreement about the ambiguity background validation introduces: we trust a snapshot enough to use it immediately, but describe that trust as temporary until the same node finishes checking history.

Multiple chainstates affect much more than snapshot loading: ordinary validation changes have to account for different chainstate roles, candidate sets, notifications, downloads, pruning, cache allocation, database lifetimes and locks.
I am not sure this amount of complexity in the most critical part of our codebase is still worth it, given that adoption [isn't where we hoped it would be](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35054#issuecomment-4468360424).
Ordinary IBD is also getting faster: #35295 is already merged, and the upcoming `pruneassumevalid` will make pruned IBD even faster.

Snapshot bootstrapping without background validation can still offer an advantage: a new node becomes usable before ordinary IBD would finish because snapshot loading time scales with the UTXO set size, while ordinary IBD time scales with the blockchain size.
Whether that is worth its maintenance cost is a fair question, and we can discuss it here or in the dedicated PR where I will propose the removal.
Even after removal, we could decide to add it back in a cleaner way, for example isolated through IPC.
This demo makes that cost, and the code we could remove, visible for that discussion.

**Background validation can be considered separately:** if we keep snapshot loading, I would prefer making its trust assumption explicit and distributing verification across ordinary IBD nodes, as proposed in #32377 and #36543.
That could give us wider independent checking of the commitment without making every snapshot user maintain a second chainstate.

Users who want to validate history themselves and transition to an archival node could rebuild with `-reindex` and pruning disabled.
Alternatively, they could run IBD in a separate datadir while their snapshot node remains usable, then switch once it is ready.
@Sjors's #36557 discusses dropping mandatory background sync and these alternatives.

**What the series demonstrates:**

* After the fixture cleanup in #36601, the next eight commits remove background validation while snapshot loading keeps working, a stopping point that can be reviewed on its own.
* The middle commits remove snapshot imports and startup resumption, then the validation, block storage, notification and release-process special cases they needed.
* The final seven commits add the simplifications this removal enables: startup in one pass, stable database ownership, one download path, a single prune height, and removal of the locks and diagnostics used to select and identify chainstates.

Ordinary validation, `-assumevalid`, pruning, `ChainstateManager` and UTXO export (`dumptxoutset`) remain.

**Related work:**

* [AJ's recent faster-loader branch](https://github.com/ajtowns/bitcoin/tree/202610-loadtxoutset-speedy) and [Sjors's chunked-import experiments](https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/tree/2026/10/utxo-coin-chunks) explore reducing import overhead while retaining snapshot support.
* #35054 contains the broader discussion about P2P snapshot distribution, its users and its costs.

pulls.title: private broadcast: Extra guard against unintended non-private broadcast of private transactions
pulls.body:
Motivation: Reduce the risk of accidental privacy leak happening when broadcasting non-privately a requested transaction that had been previously broadcast privately.

Background: During the initial phase of private broadcast implementation there were unforeseen instances when a private transaction could get broadcast non-privately (see #35032 #35319 #35410 #36309 #36312 #36277 #36330).

Currently known pathways:

- Re-submission through `submitpackage`
- Wallet-rebroadcast (when a private transaction is "picked up" by the wallet, and rebrodcast after 1-2 days)

Note that these are being addressed, but other, currently non-identified pathways cannot be excluded.

Change summary: Add a general, extra safeguard: whenever there is a transaction broadcast request, check if the given transaction has been previously broadcast privately, and if so, refuse to broadcast non-privately.

Transaction relay is not affected, as it should not be affected by private broadcast.  When we receive a previously private-broadcast transaction for the first time (it's not yet in our mempool), we relay it as any other relayed transaction. Behavior is unchanged in this regard.

Notes:

- Prerequisite: This is built on top of #36477, as keeping finished private broadcasts in the queue is a prerequisite for this change to work.
- This proposed change is not an alternative to the use-case specific safeguards, but a complementary one.
- Testing currently uses the two pathways listed above. When they are closed, testing will be more difficult (i.e., it is hard to establish whether non-private broadcast is prevented by the use-case specific or the present generic guard).
- The private broadcast queue is not persisted, it doesn't survive node restarts
- Entries deleted via `abortprivatebroadcast` will be forgotten.

Keeping as Draft, because the prerequisite #36477 is pending.

pulls.title: node: batch block file pruning in a single pass over block index
pulls.body:
When starting a node with pruning enabled (e.g. `-prune=550`) on a node with full chain history or pruning many files at once, `FindFilesToPrune` and `FindFilesToPruneManual` previously called `PruneOneBlockFile` once per file.

Because `PruneOneBlockFile` iterated over the entire `m_block_index` for each file, this was an O(M * N) operation (M = files to prune, N = total blocks). When pruning a full chain (~5,770 files and ~972k blocks), this triggered ~5.6 billion iterations and froze the node running on a Pi 5 for ~10 minutes on startup while holding `cs_main`.

This PR replaces `PruneOneBlockFile` with `PruneBlockFiles(const std::set<int>&)`, which collects all candidate files and prunes them in a single O(M + N) pass over `m_block_index` using a compact dynamic bitfield (`std::vector<bool>`). Also skips entries without block or undo data to avoid unneeded checks and prevent file 0 pruning from dirtying header-only or already-pruned index entries. The new signature is analogous to `UnlinkPrunedFiles({file_number});`.

Benchmarked with ~972k blocks and 5,770 files to prune:
- x86_64 (i7-8665U @ 1.90 GHz): 75.1s -> 14.7ms (~5,100x speedup)
- ARM64 (Raspberry Pi 5): 606.0s -> 26.3ms (>3,500x speedup)

Both timings were taken with a datadir whose block index and block file info records came from a full chain, with the `blk*.dat` and `rev*.dat` files backfilled as 0-byte files. Pruning selection reads only the index and the file info, so empty files reproduce the startup cost without a full chain, and `UnlinkPrunedFiles` deletes them cheaply.

A case where this matters in practice is a pruned node restarting after a long outage. It downloads headers for the whole gap first, leaving many header-only entries behind, then has to prune a large backlog in a few flushes. The data-less skip avoids re-dirtying all of those entries, and the single pass bounds the work by the index size instead of files times index size.

Add unit test `blockmanager_prune_block_files_batch` to verify batch pruning, empty set no-ops, clean dirty-set behavior, and cleared block and undo metadata. Add a test for the `FindFilesToPruneManual` caller path, including a mixed valid and out-of-range file set. Update caller tests in `blockmanager_tests` and `rescan_tests`.

Addition, I ran the test on my laptop as well, going from full node to `prune=5000` took 8:11:
```
2026-11-11T16:50:09Z init message: Pruning blockstore…
2026-11-11T16:58:20Z block tree size = 975494
```

pulls.title: Add output script index and corresponding script history RPC
pulls.body:
Add a new index `txoscriptindex` which indexes all output scripts. Introduce a new `getscripthistory` RPC that returns all transactions that create outputs corresponding to the provided scripts, and optionally the transactions that spend those outputs if `txospenderindex` is also configured.

This has been a long-requested feature, attempted in previous PRs (#2802, #3652, #6835, #10370, #14053).
Some concerns raised were about the ability for an index like this to scale. I think the new techniques being used to build the indexes (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35531, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002) alleviate this concern. This index can be synced in a few hours and the current disk usage is ~54 GB. This is less than the ~66 GB `txindex` disk usage in v31 and earlier. This index can also be used with a pruned node, so a full node can be supported in < 100 GB of disk space. Missing blocks are returned by hash and can be requested from peers using `getblockfrompeer`.

Some other previous concerns were more conceptual, that this type of index could encourage address reuse and chain analysis. IMO this ship has sailed, and the current status quo of not shipping an address index is turning off users who expect this functionality. Workarounds involve installing, configuring, and syncing other third-party software, making the UX of using Bitcoin Core in a self-sovereign way unnecessarily difficult.

The index hashes each output script with SHA256, then applies salted SipHash-1-3-UJ and stores a six-byte prefix. This is to support the popular Electrum protocol, which supplies only the script hash. The RPC can also look up by address or descriptors. Ranged descriptors are also supported, so a single RPC call can return the entire history of a receive/change xpub pair.

Because there are some scripts with millions of outputs, we introduce a new `OrderedVarInt` which serializes the block height after the script hash prefix. This lets LevelDB seek directly to the prefix + block height, so we can page by block height range.

To prevent DoS concerns by supplying an address with millions of outputs, the RPC tracks a byte budget of reads and throws immediately if too many reads are attempted. The error message instructs the user to narrow the block range.

Improvements to `txospenderindex` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36480) will also allow us to use that pruned. The end result would allow users to run with all optional indexes (including this one) in < 200 GB of disk space. Of course a larger pruned setting would be desired if many historical block lookups were being requested.

pulls.title: fuzz: Add a target that feeds arbitrary bytes to V2Transport
pulls.body:
No fuzz target feeds V2Transport bytes that an honest peer would not send past the v2 key exchange. I add p2p_transport_v2_receive. It knows the transport's keys, builds the input from arbitrary bytes and from parts of a valid handshake (the peer key, garbage, the terminator, encrypted packets that may be corrupted, and runs of empty decoys that force a rekey), and feeds it in pieces of arbitrary size. Once the transport reports v2, it checks that its session id matches the peer's.

It reaches the v2 receive states and their failures, except the fallback to v1 and the wrong-magic disconnect, which need a v1 `version` header at the start of the stream; `p2p_transport_bidirectional_v1v2` reaches the first. 15 minutes with libFuzzer, ASan and UBSan found no crash.

pulls.title: cli: Parse -signetchallenge like bitcoind
pulls.body:
`bitcoind` returns an useful error when invalid hex is passed to `-signetchallenge`:

```
$ bitcoind -signet -signetchallenge=z
Error: -signetchallenge must be hex, not 'z'
```

The error returned by `bitcoin-cli` only indicates that the RPC cookie wasn't found. It doesn't hint at invalid hex:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -signet -signetchallenge=z getblockcount
error: Authorization failed: ...
Is your -signetchallenge correct for custom signets?
```

To have consistent validation of signet args in `bitcoind` and `bitcoin-cli`, we now parse `-signetchallenge` in a new `ReadSignetChallengeArg()` function which is called in `GetSignetDataDir()` and `ReadSigNetArgs()`.

Addresses https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34566#discussion_r3668123074

I didn't add a release note because I don't think this change of an error message warrants one.

pulls.title: validation: don't treat snapshot block as linked on startup
pulls.body:
Background sync requests blocks up to and including the snapshot block from several peers at once, so the snapshot block can be stored before one of its ancestors. `ReceivedBlockTransactions()` then keeps it in `m_blocks_unlinked`, but that isn't persisted. On restart `LoadBlockIndex()` gives it the hardcoded `m_chain_tx_count`, `PopulateBlockIndexCandidates()` makes it a background candidate, and `FindMostWorkChain()` walks back to its parent, which has no chain tx count:

```
Assertion failed: (pindexTest->HaveNumChainTxs() || pindexTest->nHeight == 0), function FindMostWorkChain, file validation.cpp, line 3217.
```

It needs a restart in that window, so it should be rare, but after that the node aborts on every start. The only ways out I found are `-reindex-chainstate` or `-reindex`, and both delete the snapshot chainstate.

Fix this by adding the snapshot block to `m_blocks_unlinked` on startup if an ancestor is missing, and not making it a background candidate until then. Both are needed, without the first one background validation stalls. A node that is already stuck starts with the fix and finishes background validation without a reindex.

The new step in `feature_assumeutxo.py` restarts the node after the snapshot block is submitted out of order, and fails on master. I also reproduced it over p2p with a test peer that withholds the snapshot block's parent.

These are the two changes from #35307 (closed, the motivation there was `submitblock` before `loadtxoutset`) without its blockfile and VerifyDB changes. cyb3ralbert hit the same assertion while testing #36452 (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36452#issuecomment-6464524112), which is still needed when the snapshot tip is at the snapshot block. #36149 drops the `BLOCK_HAVE_DATA` check in the branch right below, so whichever is merged second should match it.

pulls.title: validation: delete pruned files after a failed flush
pulls.body:
If a flush that prunes block files fails before the block index write, the files are already marked pruned in memory, but `setFilesToPrune` is a local in `FlushStateToDisk()`. The next successful flush writes the pruned file info and never deletes the blk/rev files. Only `ScanAndUnlinkAlreadyPrunedFiles()` deletes them, at the next startup.

This is number 7 of ryanofsky's [post-merge review of #35714](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35714#pullrequestreview-5697890316). The block file flush failure from #35714 and the blocks directory `CheckDiskSpace()` failure both return before that write.

I worked on this because it lets me test my kernel pruning refactor (#36738, for #35627 and kernel-node/kernel-node#111) against the issue he describes. The refactor moves the flush, block index write and file deletion that a pruning flush runs from `FlushStateToDisk()` into `WriteBlockStorage()`, and no unit test ran that sequence in prune mode. I rebased the refactor onto this branch, and the new tests pass on each of its commits.

The first three commits add tests that pass on master. The unit test fixtures apply `-prune` and `-fastprune` from `extra_args`, `chainstate_flush_failure_boundary` checks that a flush after a failed one writes what was skipped, and `prune_flush_failure` shows that a failed prune flush still leaves its files on disk after a retry.

The last commit keeps the selected files in `BlockManager` and deletes them after the next block index write. If that write fails they are dropped with the dirty entries, which means a file is only deleted once it is marked pruned on disk. Pending files don't force a write. The next flush that writes deletes them.

The disk-space failure and automatic pruning take the same path but have no test. Neither does the `FindNextBlockPos()` line that drops a file from the pending set when a block is written to it, which can happen after an assumeutxo snapshot validates.

pulls.title: GUARDED_BY annotations for nTx, m_chain_tx_count
pulls.body: The cs_main requirement was never made explicit. The nTx field is modified when the block data is received and m_chain_tx_count is modified when all ancestors' block data has been received. Because of this, reading nTx from the getblockheader RPC may race as it does not acquire cs_main. Also, m_chain_tx_count may race in getchaintxstats if a pruned node redownloads a block via getblockfrompeer or if the node is running assumeutxo and tries to read m_chain_tx_count while it is being written to.

pulls.title: qa: check more socket API invariants for each platform we support
pulls.body:
This improves our `Sock` test coverage following CVE-2026-117350.

This leaves out the test for the specific case that led to the OOM until we [fix `select()` reporting](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36688#issue-6085527087) for urgent data, but i'm also trying not to fight the last battle too much. Instead i focused on trying to pin down all invariants Claude and I could come up with that could be reasonably tested. This will help us understand our code better, and get more assurance we do not break some assumption a (security critical) caller may be relying on further down the road.

Another goal is to tie the events our fuzzing mock can report to the events each OS actually reports, and when. A follow-up will extend the mock to match what these tests pin down. This wouldn’t have caught the CVE-2026-117350 bug: it was in the very logic the mock replaces, so a fuzz target could only have found it if the mock had been written with that bug in mind. But the next bug may well be somewhere else, and a mock that can report everything the real socket APIs can, lets the fuzzer reach corner cases which may lack a proper unit test.

A lot more coverage could be added. I chose not to add tests specific to the logic used for trusted interfaces (Tor control, the SOCKS5 proxy, I2P SAM) or to a single platform. I also left out the test which led me to find https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36688#issuecomment-6509375262, as this needs to be fixed first.
